200	Sales should be done on Shabbatot; on weekdays, don't sell them, give them out to people, so that the poorer worshippers
201	can also give.
202	And you'll say, yes, but there's the wealthy man, there are always two or three millionaires in a synagogue, and he
203	buys for this one and buys for that one, but he doesn't feel comfortable that they bought for him, he feels he has to pay it back,
204	so in any case, if you don't sell them, then never bring secular people
205	to one of the seven aliyot. Not one of the seven. No. Or rather, the best
206	is Petichat HaHechal, Hagbahah. After all, they're strong, they go to the gym, they have muscles. Hagbahah,
207	let them do Hagbahah, Petichat HaHechal, Rimonim. Among the Ashkenazim they also have Gelilah.
208	Gelilah, excellent. That way they'll lift them up, and they'll also tell them: "Happy are you, how did you merit this?" Gelilah is equal to all of them.
209	You can do another seven. You can add another seven. Actually, you can add another hundred.
210	Why?
211	Because after all, this is what we do on Simchat Torah, we add as many as we want. We just can't tire out the congregation. So
212	Rav Ovadia said we shouldn't add more aliyot: on Yom Tov no more than five, on Yom Kippur
213	no more than six, on Shabbat no more than seven.
214	Right, yes, you can do it that way. Yes, yes, that's best.
215	In any case, do we let him do "Yimloch"?
216	Very nice.
217	So that's the problem, because the Ben Ish Chai writes: say you give him the honor of "Yimloch," and he doesn't believe in it, he
218	won't reign, but he desecrates Shabbat.
219	For example, the Ben Ish Chai writes: do not call up a public Shabbat desecrator to the aliyah of "those who desecrate it shall surely be put to death."
220	Why? If you asked me, with my little brain, I'd say: call him up next, so he'll see what happens
221	to someone who does this. But the Ben Ish Chai writes that it's a problem, because after all you're shaming him in front of everyone.
222	So even a secular person, it's forbidden to shame him in front of everyone. So writes the Ben Ish Chai. A man who has relations with a niddah, and it's known
223	that his wife doesn't keep family purity, they don't call him up to the passage about the niddah.
224	Or all kinds of things like that. You have to be careful.
225	Today, who pays attention?
226	The reader of the Torah barely knows what the next aliyah is, and nobody knows, so everyone goes up, and even if people pay
227	attention, believe me, even this secular man who goes up and reads "those who desecrate it shall surely be put to death," his head is totally in Bloomfield.
228	Where is his head?
229	Do you think he notices what he is reading in the Torah?
230	They don't pay attention, they don't even stumble.
231	So there is a dispute. Rav Ovadia, you often see a secular man going up, he looks at
232	it, the blemish.
233	He doesn't know what "mumim" means.
234	So Rav Mashash writes that even if he doesn't open his mouth and read, it's still fine.
235	Why?
236	By the law of "shome'a ke'oneh" (hearing is like responding).
237	Rosh Hashanah 29.
238	But Rav Ovadia says it doesn't help,
239	"shome'a ke'oneh" here.
